title: Store by Frequency of Use
subtitle: Every keeper has a home; now place the homes by how often you reach for them. Prime space is expensive, so spend it on what you use most and send the rare things a step further off.
part_position: Second chapter of Part Four (Straighten), chapters 12 to 15; continues the second of the six S's and takes the second Straighten step
hands_off_note: Chapter 14 keeps working inside Straighten: the homes are assigned and now well placed, but a good spot is obvious only to the person who set it up, so the next chapter makes each home clear at a glance with a label, an outline, or a simple visual cue, so anyone can find and return a thing without asking.
audience: Readers who have just finished Chapter 12 and given every keeper a home, and are standing at the entryway where four keepers hang on four identical hooks and the mail sits in its tray, each home well built but every one treated the same. Busy home keepers and parents. Applying the method, not new to it. They do not need to re-assign homes; they need to place each home by how often they reach for it, so the busiest things hold the best spots.
core_promise: Continue the second S by placing each already-assigned home according to how often you use it, spending your scarce, expensive, easy-to-reach space on your busiest things. Name the prime zone, the small band of genuinely effortless reach measured from where you use a thing, and sort each keeper into a rough tier, daily to the prime zone, weekly near, rare a step further off. Audit the best spots you already own, free the ones being wasted, and store each thing at its point of use, so reaching gets cheaper for the things you reach for most and the room quietly speeds up, all without adding or removing a single thing.
emotional_purpose: Keep the lighter Straighten mood going. Placing homes by frequency is arranging, not agonizing, and wrong placement is a fixable first draft, not a personal failing. Lift any blame from the things hogging the good spots, because nobody put them there as a character flaw; they simply landed and never moved. Deliver the honest second-Straighten-step milestone without overselling it: the room got easier even though nothing left the house, and the goal is still ahead.
practical_purpose: Draw the line between assigning a home (already done in Chapter 12) and placing it well (today's only job); state the principle that prime space is expensive, so spend it on what you use every day and send the once-a-year things a step further off; teach the prime zone as the small, scarce band of easy reach measured from where you stand; give the one rule, the best spot goes to the thing you reach for most; teach the daily/weekly/rare tiers and where each goes; audit the best spots for things that never earned them and store each thing at its point of use, not where it belongs on a list; walk the entryway keepers into placements by frequency, then scale to the kitchen cabinet and the coat closet; and read the friction meter as the second Straighten step.
primary_cta: Open one drawer or cabinet you use every day, find the thing in the easiest-to-reach spot that you almost never use, and trade it with a daily thing that is currently awkward to get to. One swap, and the space is faster. Read the chapter free in the online book.
secondary_cta: Read the chapter free online, then continue to Chapter 14, where Straighten keeps working: the homes are assigned and now well placed, but a good spot is obvious only to the person who set it up, so the next chapter makes each home clear at a glance with a label, an outline, or a simple visual cue.

secondary_device: The core principle, prime space is expensive, so spend it on what you use every day and send the once-a-year things a step further off, paired with the one rule that the best spot goes to the thing you reach for most, and the point-of-use reframe that a spot is measured from your hand at the moment you need the thing, not from a tidy category on a list; each home is placed by the daily/weekly/rare tiers

worked_example.space: the settled entryway from Chapter 12, where four keepers hang on four identical hooks at the same prime height with tomorrow's mail in a tray below, each home well built but every one treated the same, now placed by how often the hand goes to it
worked_example.note: The entryway is a small space full of mostly frequent things, so its tiering is gentle and the differences are inches; the principle earns its keep in fuller rooms, so it is scaled up to the kitchen cabinet and the coat closet. Nothing is added and nothing is carried out; only the placements change, so the busiest things become the easiest to reach.

items.keys: THE prime spot, the hook or tray closest to the door at hand height, the very first thing your hand meets on the way in, because nothing here is touched more, going out and back many times a day.
items.leash: Also prime, right up front beside the keys, because it goes out and back with the dog morning and evening, just as often as the keys, no drawer and no fishing.
items.reusable_bag: Near rather than prime, a hook just to the side, because you take it a few times a week rather than a few times a day, still an easy grab on the way out but no longer holding a front-row seat it does not fill.
items.umbrella: A step further off, into a stand in the corner or onto a lower hook, because it works hard on a rainy day and does nothing on the many dry ones, close enough to grab when the sky turns and out of the way the rest of the time.
items.outgoing_mail: Right in the exit path, because it is brief but constant, in your hand for two seconds on the way out, so it rides out with you instead of sinking into a pile.

worked_example.scaling_up: The kitchen cabinet, where the mugs and plates you use every morning come to the front at eye-to-waist height in the prime zone and the once-a-year roasting pan goes up top where the rare reach costs almost nothing; and the coat closet, where the jackets you actually wear this week hang at the front and the out-of-season coats get slid to the ends until their season comes around.
worked_example.tally: Same keepers, same room, nothing added or removed, but the placements now match how often each thing is used, so the keys and leash hold the best spots, the bag sits a step to the side, the umbrella waits in its corner, and the mail rides the exit path. Reaching got cheaper for the things you reach for most, and the entryway is quicker to use than it was an hour ago.

definition: Storing by frequency of use means placing each home by how often you reach for it: daily things in the prime, easy-reach space, weekly things near, and rare or seasonal things a step further off. The more you use it, the closer and easier it goes.
one_idea_to_keep: Match the reach to the use. The things your hand wants a dozen times a day should be the easiest to reach; the things you want once a year can afford to be a stretch. Spend your best space on your busiest things, and the room quietly speeds up.

the three loose tiers, sorted rough not exact: daily to the prime zone, weekly near, rare a step further off; the more often you use a thing, the closer and easier its home should be
frequency placement is a first draft, not a test you can fail: the room announces where you guessed wrong and sliding a thing one shelf over costs nothing

store it where you use it, not where it belongs on a list; the point of use beats the tidy category every time, because you live at the point of use and only visit the category
